clue.text: Mark — a book written about start of Christian church ...

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
a phrase written about something is written all round it, so the outer pair goes around the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
NT is the New Testament, the usual crossword book
its opening letter
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: The Gospel of Mark described as a book about the beginnings of the Christian church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A book' is treated as one unit with a gap in the middle. 'Mark' looks like the evangelist and his gospel, but it is the ordinary noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An accent is a mark placed over a letter, such as an acute or grave, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Plant making ammo exploding in the country

indicators.note: ammunition that explodes is blown apart, so its letters land in a new order
in puts the rearranged letters inside the country's name

blocks.note: the South American country
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A factory turning out ammunition that blows up somewhere in the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a factory making ammunition, but it is the herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Chamomile is a daisy-like herb grown for tea, so it is an example of a plant.

clue.text: Ideal husband no longer generous

blocks.note: a husband no longer is an ex-husband, an ex
a generous helping is an ample one

explanation.surface: A perfect husband who has stopped being openhanded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ideal husband' reads as one phrase, after Wilde's play, but 'Ideal' is the definition, used as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal, as a noun, is a model to follow, which is what an example set for others is.

clue.text: Duck hiding tail in the drink

indicators.note: a bird hiding its tail has its last part out of sight, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: the teal is a small duck

explanation.surface: A duck tucking its tail away as it sits on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the drink' is slang for in the water, which hides that 'drink' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is a hot beverage, so it is an example of a drink.

clue.text: ... sometime after King Edward backed Wycliffe, say

indicators.note: something backed has been sent the wrong way, so the king's letters are read right to left
after tells us which piece comes second when the two are joined end to end

blocks.note: Edwardus Rex, the royal cipher, abbreviated
sometime as an adjective means one-time or previous

explanation.surface: A church history: something happening at some point after a King Edward, concerning Wycliffe.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots tie this to the previous clue in the surface only; the wordplay is complete on its own. 'Sometime' looks like an adverb of time but works as the adjective meaning one-time.
explanation.definitionFit: John Wycliffe was a fourteenth-century critic of the Church, an example of a religious reformer before the Reformation.

clue.text: Unnamed anthem used in extremely rude poem

indicators.note: unnamed means without its N, the abbreviation for name, so that letter is taken off
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are kept
used in puts the shortened song inside the pair of end letters

blocks.note: its first and last letters
a hymn is a song of praise, an anthem

explanation.surface: An anonymous anthem worked into an obscene verse.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the standard abbreviation for name, so 'unnamed' takes an N away.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhyme is a short verse, as in a nursery rhyme, so it can stand for a poem.

clue.text: Resisting attack very well

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: in shape for fighting off an assault
second meaning: in excellent health

explanation.walkthrough: The first half takes the phrase literally, fit to be fighting; the second is its everyday sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in peak health, and taken word by word it describes someone in condition for combat.

clue.text: So-called private resentment

indicators.note: so-called points to what a word is called, that is how it is said, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: a private soldier serves in the ranks, so is a ranker

explanation.surface: Bitterness someone keeps to themselves, or a grudge passed off as private.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like an adjective about keeping a grudge to oneself, but it is the army rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancour is long-lasting bitterness and ill will, a close synonym of resentment.

clue.text: Return uplifted from great celebration

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow
in a down clue, lifting letters up reads them from the bottom, so backwards

blocks.note: the letters running across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Coming home on a high after a big party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' reads as coming back, but it is the verb for voting someone into office.
explanation.definitionFit: To return a candidate is to elect them to Parliament, as in a constituency returning its member.

clue.text: Talk idly in one language or another

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other, which is the casing for it

blocks.note: Malay is the language of Malaysia
to gas is to chatter at length about nothing

explanation.surface: Someone chattering away idly in one tongue or another.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is just 'another', borrowing 'language' from the wordplay before it. Malagasy is the language of Madagascar.
explanation.definitionFit: Malagasy is the national tongue of Madagascar, so it is one more language beside Malay.

clue.text: Dope visibly embarrassed about sex

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the colour word is read backwards

blocks.note: dope and gen both mean inside information
someone blushing is red in the face

explanation.surface: A fool blushing when the subject of sex comes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' reads as an idiot, but it means information, as gen does in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Sex and gender are both used for the category of male or female on a form.

clue.text: Praise from pulpit oddly cutting say

indicators.note: oddly keeps the letters in the odd-numbered places: first, third, fifth
a piece cutting another splits it open and sits inside it

blocks.note: to comment is to say something
letters one, three and five

explanation.surface: A preacher handing out praise from the pulpit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' sits at the end looking like 'for example', but it is the verb that gets cut open.
explanation.definitionFit: A compliment is an expression of praise or admiration, so the noun is a synonym.

clue.text: Persistent misuse of utopian term

indicators.note: a misuse of something puts it to the wrong use, so its letters go the wrong way

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps on misusing the word utopian.
explanation.definitionFit: An importunate person pesters with repeated demands, so is persistent to the point of annoyance.

clue.text: Reluctant to drop line — this word must be kept

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it fall out, so one letter leaves the word

blocks.note: loath means unwilling
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Someone unwilling to drop a line of text, insisting the wording stays.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase: a word that must be kept is a promise.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath is a solemn promise, someone's word, and a promise is something one must keep.

clue.text: Swimmer's position when diving

blocks.note: first meaning: a predatory freshwater fish
second meaning: the body bent at the hips with legs straight

explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the swimmer a person at a pool; it is a fish, and the diving position is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The fish and the jackknife shape used in diving and gymnastics share one name.

clue.text: What's never odd or even in random pile, possibly?

definitions.text: What's never odd or even in random pile, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements the letters could take

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A riddle about something neither odd nor even, found in a random heap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Never odd or even' reads the same both ways, so it is a famous example of the answer, and the whole clue defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: A palindrome reads identically forwards and backwards, which the quoted phrase does letter for letter.

clue.text: Open country in spring not quiet

indicators.note: not tells us the quiet letter is left out

blocks.note: to spring is to leap
p is piano, the musical marking for quiet

explanation.surface: Countryside in springtime without any noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season, but it is the verb to jump.
explanation.definitionFit: A lea is a poetic word for meadow or grassland, which is open country.

clue.text: Festival sign put up round artist's quarters

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting letters up reverses their order
the lodgings go round the artist, who sits inside them

blocks.note: the Ram is Aries, a sign of the zodiac
digs is British slang for lodgings
RA, Royal Academician, is the usual artist

explanation.surface: A festival banner hung up around a painter's lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artist's quarters' gives the artist placed inside the lodgings. Digs is British slang for rented rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: Mardi Gras is the carnival held on Shrove Tuesday, before Lent, so it is a festival.

clue.text: Husband with cap is a rugby player

blocks.note: to cap a story is to better or outdo it
a half is a back such as a scrum half or fly half

explanation.surface: A husband who has won an international cap for his country at rugby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cap' looks like a sporting honour, but it is the verb meaning outdo. A rugby half plays behind the scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My better half' is a jokey idiom for one's spouse, so a husband can be called one.

clue.text: Time needed with old-fashioned drawing tool

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
someone square is conventional and out of date

explanation.surface: Taking your time with an antique piece of drafting equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old-fashioned' seems to describe the tool, but it is the word square.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-square is a T-shaped ruler used by draughtsmen to draw straight horizontal lines.

clue.text: Severe cut some announced

indicators.note: as some people say it aloud, so the sound matters, in an accent that drops the r

blocks.note: to saw is to cut through wood

explanation.surface: A drastic reduction that a few people made public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' limits the sound match to speakers who do not sound the r, for whom saw and the answer are alike, as in much of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Sore can mean grave or harsh, as in 'in sore need' or 'a sore trial', close to severe.

clue.text: Love match after second minute

indicators.note: after places the pairing word behind the pieces named next

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second
minute, meaning tiny, is wee
a tie is a cup match

explanation.surface: A love match that follows a second meeting after just a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love match' reads as a romance, but 'Love' alone is the endearment and 'match' is a fixture. Wee is Scots and British for small.
explanation.definitionFit: Love and sweetie are both terms of endearment used when speaking to someone dear.

clue.text: Island state without soldiers rebuffed republic nearby

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the soldiers are taken out of the state
rebuffed suggests being pushed back, so what remains is read in the other direction

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for island
the Gulf state
the TA is the Territorial Army

explanation.surface: An island nation without an army spurned by a neighbouring republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Island state' reads as one thing, but the island is just I and the state is the Gulf emirate. The TA is Britain's reserve army.
explanation.definitionFit: Iraq is a republic in the Gulf region, near the emirate used in the wordplay.

clue.text: Care taken about horse's capabilities

indicators.note: taken about suggests being turned around and moved, so the letters are reshuffled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: Looking after a horse according to what it can do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' is slang for heroin, which is abbreviated H.
explanation.definitionFit: Reach is the extent of someone's power or ability, as in 'beyond my reach', so it means capabilities.

clue.text: Unresolved position of hawk or dove?

blocks.note: first meaning: still undecided
second meaning, read literally: where a flying bird is

explanation.walkthrough: Hawks and doves suggest political hardliners and peacemakers, but the second half means the birds in flight.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means not yet settled, and literally it is where a bird is when aloft.

clue.text: Boy swallowing large malt from here!

definitions.note: a place, defined as where a malt comes from

indicators.note: something swallowing another takes it inside, so the outer word goes around

blocks.note: 'Boy!' and 'I say!' are both exclamations of surprise
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A lad knocking back a big glass of malt whisky, exclaiming where it comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boy' looks like a lad, but it is the exclamation. Islay is a Scottish island known for its peaty single-malt whiskies.
explanation.definitionFit: Islay, an island in the Inner Hebrides, has many distilleries, so it is a place malt whisky comes from.

clue.text: Articles at front of bag that may be unzipped

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept
the articles are placed at the bag's opening letter, which leads

blocks.note: its first letter
three articles: an, an and a

explanation.surface: Items packed into the front pocket of a zip-up bag.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic hint: the fruit is opened by peeling a strip down its length, like undoing a zip.
explanation.definitionFit: A banana is peeled in strips from the top down, which can be likened to unzipping it.

clue.text: Bond story involving revolver and spinning game

indicators.note: a spinning thing turns round, so the game's letters are read backwards
involving means taking in, so the story wraps around the other pieces

blocks.note: a story can be a fib
gat is gangster slang for a gun
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A James Bond plot featuring a gun and a spinning game of chance.
explanation.walkthrough: Bond, a revolver and a spinning game suggest 007 and Russian roulette; 'Bond' is just a tie.
explanation.definitionFit: A ligature is anything used to tie or bind, such as a cord, so it is a bond.

clue.text: Perform live in boat or carriage

blocks.note: first meaning: play a concert date, as musicians do
second meaning: a light rowing boat, or a light two-wheeled horse-drawn cart

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is itself two meanings, both covered by one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Musicians gig when they play a show, and the word also names a light ship's boat and a one-horse carriage.

clue.text: Butcher hit by the ultimately perfect crime

indicators.note: to butcher something is to hack it about, so the letters are mangled into a new order
ultimately points to the end, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
its final letter
very as an adjective means exact or perfect, as in 'the very thing'

explanation.surface: A butcher struck down in what turns out to be the perfect crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher' looks like a person, the victim, but it is a verb telling us to mangle the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Thievery is the act of stealing, which is a crime.

clue.text: Rock's enjoyable on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio we only hear words, so sound is what counts

blocks.note: enjoyable means nice

explanation.surface: Rock music that sounds good when broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' suggests music on the radio, but it is geology; the G of this word is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Gneiss is a banded metamorphic stone, so it is a type of rock.
